title: Closures & Lexical Scope
summary: A closure is a function bundled with the environment it was defined in — the mechanism that makes callbacks, memoization, and private state without classes actually work under the hood.

slides.markdown:
A **closure** is a function paired with the environment — the variables — it had access to when it was defined, even after that outer scope has finished running. It's the mechanism, not a feature you opt into: any language with [first-class functions](higher-order-functions-and-composition) has closures, whether or not the term ever comes up.

Closures are why the higher-order functions from the previous topic actually work in practice. A callback passed to an event handler, a `map` call using a variable from the enclosing function, a memoization cache — all of these are a function silently carrying its defining scope with it.

This topic is also where a classic interview bug lives: three callbacks that all print the same wrong value, because they closed over a shared variable instead of a per-iteration one.

Precisely: a closure is a function value plus a reference to the **lexical environment** in which it was created — the set of variables that were in scope at its definition site, not at its call site.

`def make_adder(n): return lambda x: x + n` — calling `make_adder(5)` returns a function. That function is a closure: it's the lambda `lambda x: x + n`, bundled with a reference to `n = 5`, which it captured from `make_adder`'s local scope. Calling the returned function later, from anywhere, still sees `n = 5`, even though `make_adder`'s call has long since returned and its stack frame is gone.

The key word is **reference**, not copy: if the captured variable is later reassigned (in languages that allow that), the closure sees the new value — it didn't snapshot `n` at creation time, it kept a live link to the variable itself.

slides.sectionTitle: A scope that outlives its function
slides.markdown:
The counter-intuitive part: an outer function's local variables normally die when it returns. A closure is the exception — if any inner function still references them, the runtime keeps them alive.

![A captured variable surviving on the heap after its outer function frame is gone, because the closure still references it](assets/closure-heap-survival.svg)

Mechanically, this is why languages with closures can't simply pop a stack frame and forget it: the compiler has to detect which local variables are captured by an inner function and allocate those specifically on the heap (or in a separate captured-variables cell) instead of the stack, so they survive after the frame that created them is gone.

assets.alt: A captured variable surviving on the heap after its outer function frame is gone, because the closure still references it

slides.subTitle: makeCounter()

slides.markdown:
**Lexical scoping** means a variable reference resolves based on *where the code is written* — its position in the source — not where or how the function is eventually called. The alternative, **dynamic scoping**, resolves a variable against the caller's environment at call time; it's rare in mainstream languages today (some Lisps and shell scripting use it) precisely because it makes a function's behavior depend on its caller's local variables, which is hard to reason about.

Concretely: a function defined inside `outer` that references `outer`'s local variable `x` will always resolve `x` to *that* `x`, no matter which other function calls it from wherever, with whatever variables of its own also happen to be named `x`. The nesting in the source code is what matters, permanently, once the function is defined.

This is precisely what makes closures possible and predictable: the captured variables are determined by the *text* of the program, so you can know exactly what a function closes over just by reading it, without tracing every call site.

slides.sectionTitle: What closures are used for in real code
slides.markdown:
Three practical uses, all of which you've almost certainly written without naming them:

- **Memoization.** A cache variable captured by an inner function that checks it before recomputing: `def memoize(fn): cache = {}; def wrapper(x): ...; return wrapper` — `cache` lives in `memoize`'s closure, invisible outside it, persisting across every call to the returned `wrapper`.
- **Private state without a class.** The `makeCounter` pattern — encapsulation via scope instead of via access modifiers, common in JavaScript before classes were idiomatic and still common in functional code today.
- **Event-handler and callback factories.** `make_click_handler(item_id)` returning a function that already knows which `item_id` it's handling, so the DOM or framework doesn't need to pass it back in — the handler closes over exactly the context it needs.

All three share the same shape: a factory function creates and returns an inner function, and the inner function's closure is what carries the state or configuration forward.

Because a closure keeps its captured variables alive for as long as the closure itself is reachable, capturing more than you need can hold memory hostage.

A real pattern: a callback captures an entire large object — say, a full API response — just to read one field from it inside a long-lived event listener. As long as that listener is registered, the *whole* object stays in memory, not just the field, because the closure's captured environment is the variable, not a value you pulled out of it. Register a few hundred such listeners over a session (common in long-running single-page apps) and you have a slow, hard-to-spot memory leak — the objects look unreferenced everywhere except inside closures nobody's looking at.

The fix is disciplined capture: read out only the specific field you need into a small local before the closure is created, or explicitly null out/unsubscribe the listener when it's no longer needed, rather than trusting garbage collection to clean up a reference chain that's still technically live.

Both hide state behind an interface — the question is which fits the situation:

| | Closure (factory function) | Object (class with private field) |
|---|---|---|
| State shape | usually one or a few variables | arbitrary, structured fields |
| Multiple methods sharing state | awkward — return an object of functions, or one dispatch function | natural — each method is a class member |
| Serialization / introspection | hard — a captured variable isn't inspectable from outside | straightforward — fields can be enumerated, logged, serialized |
| Boilerplate for one behavior | minimal — one function, one variable | a whole class declaration |
| Idiomatic in | JavaScript, Python, functional languages generally | Java, C++, most OOP-first languages |

The practical rule of thumb: reach for a closure when you need one piece of hidden state behind one or two functions; reach for a class when you need several methods sharing a richer, inspectable shape of state.

slides.sectionTitle: Debugging the classic bug on the spot
slides.markdown:
When an interviewer shows you three callbacks printing the same final value, the fluent answer names the mechanism, not just the fix: "all three closures captured the *same variable*, not three separate values, so by the time they run — after the loop has finished — they all read whatever that one variable ended up holding."

Then name two fixes and their trade-off: switch to a block-scoped binding (`let` in JS, or the language's equivalent) so each iteration gets its own variable — the cleanest fix when available — or, in a language/context without block scoping, wrap the loop body in a function call that takes the loop variable as a parameter, forcing a fresh copy per iteration the old-fashioned way.

The deeper point worth saying out loud: this isn't a JavaScript quirk, it's what lexical scoping plus a mutable shared variable always does. Any language where a loop variable is one mutable binding shared across iterations has the same bug available, which is exactly why `let`-style per-iteration bindings became the default in every modern language design.
